--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: 'Distance Sampling' slide-number: true echo: false lang: en --- # Introduction {visibility="hidden"} ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 160%;"}
**Distance sampling** ![](figs/book1){height="13cm"} ![](figs/book2){height="13cm"}
## Estimating abundance ::: {style='font-size: 90%;'} Abundance estimation is often accomplished using this equation: $$ \hat{N} = \frac{n}{\hat{p}} $$ - $N$ is abundance (population size) - $n$ is the number of individuals detected - $\hat{p}$ is an estimate of detection probability: The probability of detecting an *individual* ::: ::: {.fragment}
**Most methods differ in how they estimate $p$**
::: ## Estimating abundance Challenges: ::: {.incremental} - Detection probability is rarely constant - It is a function of: * Age * Sex * Habitat * **Distance** ::: ## Distance Sampling ::: {style='font-size: 75%;'} Basic idea: - $p_i$ is the probability of detecting individual $i$ at distance $x_i$. ::: {.fragment} - Since every individual in the population has a different detection probability, we replace $p$ with the *average* detection probability ($\bar{p}$) ::: ::: {.fragment} - The equation is now: $$ \hat{N} = \frac{n}{\hat{\bar{p}}} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} Advantages of distance sampling: - Population size can be estimated from a single survey - Explicit link between population size and density ::: ::: ## Design ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} - Randomly place line transects or points throughout the study area - Record the distance to each animal detected ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} Line transects ![](figs/fig9-7.jpg) ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} Point transects ![](figs/fig9-9.jpg) ::: ::: ::: # Line transects ## Line transects ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
![](figs/fig9-1.jpg){width="50%"}
In line transect sampling, it is common to record the radial distance and bearing, rather than the perpendicular distance. ::: {.fragment} However, the analysis must be conducted on the perpendicular distance data. ::: ::: ## Real design
Mongolian gazelle (*Procapra gutturosa*)
::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='55%'} ![](figs/Kirk.jpg) ::: ::: {.column width='45%'} ![](figs/Book_of_antelopes_(1894)_Gazella_gutturosa) ::: ::: ## Line transects ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} Animal | Distance ($x$) ------ | ------------- 1 | 4.4 2 | 25.3 3 | 41.8 4 | 3.1 5 | 78.5 $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ $n$ | 4.4 ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} ![](figs/example1) ::: ::: ## [Estimating average detection probability]{style="font-size: 75%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Fit a detection function, $\mathrm{g}(x)$, to the data ::: {.fragment} Assume individuals are "uniformly" distributed with respect to the transect (valid under random sampling): $p(x) = 1/B$ where $B$ is the transect half-width. ::: ::: {.fragment} $\bar{p}$ is then the average detection function, weighted by $p(x)$. $$\bar{p} = \int_0^B g(x)p(x) \mathrm{d} x$$. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-distance-sampling_files/figure-revealjs/detfuns-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## [Computing average detection probability]{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.r-stack} ::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1} ![](figs/detfun0-0){height="13cm"} ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1} ![](figs/detfun0-1){height="13cm"} ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2} ![](figs/detfun0-2){height="13cm"} ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3} ![](figs/detfun0-3){height="13cm"} ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4} ![](figs/detfun1){height="13cm"} ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5} ![](figs/detfun2){height="13cm"} ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=6} ![](figs/detfun3){height="13cm"} ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=7} ![](figs/detfun4){height="13cm"} ::: :::
##
::: {.r-fit-text} [Shiny App](https://richard-chandler.shinyapps.io/distance-sampling/) ::: ## Assumptions ::: {style='font-size: 90%;'} ::: {.incremental} 1. Animals on the line are detected with certainty (i.e., $p=1$ when distance=0). 2. Animals do not move during the survey 3. Distance is measured accurately 4. Transect lines are placed randomly with respect to the animals * This ensures that individuals will be uniformly distributed with respect to the transect 5. Detections (of individuals or groups) are independent of one another ::: ::: # Point transects ## Point transects
![](figs/fig9-8.jpg){width="80%"}
## [Differences between point vs line transects]{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} We still use the same type of detection function (half-normal, hazard, etc...).
::: {.fragment} We don't expect a "flat" histogram of distances when $\bar{p}=1$. Why? :::
::: {.fragment} More individuals occur far from the observer than close to the observer because area increases with distance. ::: ::: ## Point Transects When average detection probability is 1, the histogram of distances will look like this because there is more area (and hence more individuals) far from the point.
![](figs/detfun5){width="40%"}
## Point Transects If average detection probability is less than 1, the histogram will increase and then decline.
![](figs/detfun6){width="40%"}
## Point Transects The fitted curve will look like this
![](figs/detfun7){width="40%"}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
